comments.text:
I think most major composers have their "signature" chords or progressions - Chopin and the V13 chord, Schumann and the circle of fifths progression in 7th chords, Scriabin and augmented chords (or the mystic chord later on), Ravel and chromatic mediant modulations, and of course Rachmaninoff and the flat 6th. When you play a lot of music from one composer yourself, you start to notice these 'cliches' - though one of the things that differentiates great composers from the good ones is that they can use these cliches without them feeling stale.

PS Your instructive analogies are a pleasure - each video you surpass yourself!

comments.text:
Thank you for your insightful analysis! Another powerful climax is the one from the 3rd movement of his cello sonata, when the main theme in Eb major returns towards the end. There is a buildup using a pattern close to the circle of fifths. The bass notes are Eb - F - Bb - G - C - F - Bb - G - C, and then we suddenly get an unexpected Emin chord. Although it doesn't quite follow the patterns you showed, Emin does contain a B natural, which is the lowered 6th in the Eb key, and is kind of like the Neapolitan sixth with inverted modes (Eb - Emin as opposed to Ebmin - E). 

Rachmaninoff also used the same trick in the middle section of his prelude Op. 23 no. 4 in D major, with an Eb - Emin chord progression marked with fortissimo at bar 50

These two examples are for me both at the emotional antipode of your Rach 3 triumphant ending example and harmonically they use the same Neapolitan chord idea, but with opposite modes :) 

Also for me the darkest sequence of chords is not the Neapolitan sixth cadence, but minor chords separated by a minor sixth (e.g. Emin - Cmin)
